clip_narrations: In nineteen ninety-nine at Harvard, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris ran a simple test. Volunteers counted passes between players in white shirts.
A person in a dark gorilla suit walked right through the game. She beat her chest for nine seconds, yet half the viewers missed her.
Viewers wrote down fifteen passes and swore no gorilla ever crossed the hall. Then they watched the tape again in total shock.
Your eyes take in the whole room at once, but your mind can only track one small target. For your brain, this is a total nightmare.
Instead of showing you everything in front of your face, your mind acts like a strict bouncer. It blocks whatever you are not hunting for.
First, light from both the players and the dark gorilla reaches your visual cortex, the vision center at the back of your brain.
Next, while you count white shirts, your parietal cortex narrows its attention spotlight onto white shapes and shuts out the dark gorilla.
Finally, eye cameras proved that people who missed the gorilla stared straight at her furry chest. They looked for one full second and saw nothing.
The researchers were left completely stunned. When they hid a gorilla in lung scans, eighty-three percent of expert doctors looked right past it too.
Which proves that staring straight at something does not mean you see it. Your mind erases giant hazards whenever you lock onto one task.
